title: AI could force rates up but jobs look safe for now: RBA
full_text:
The AI building boom that is powering the global economy could force interest rates to remain higher, the Reserve Bank's chief economist has warned, while revealing there are few signs the new technology will eat into the job prospects of young Australians.
Sarah Hunter, in an address to the UBS Australasia conference in Sydney yesterday, said AI was already having a major impact on the Australian economy: investment in data centres is up 10-fold in the past three years and there are signs they are competing with the construction sector for trade workers.
Data centre construction alone could be the equivalent of 2 per cent of GDP for the next two years, but their demand on the energy grid could force up power prices.
The size of the AI boom has caught the Reserve and other central banks by surprise. Last week, the RBA forecast that business investment would climb by 12 per cent this year. In May, it had forecast growth of just 0.8 per cent.
Proponents describe AI as a transformative general purpose technology, similar to the advent of railways and electricity.
Hunter said AI could lift productivity and transform workplaces while increasing household and business spending.
She likened the current boom to the rollout of the internet in the late 1990s and early 2000s, saying this had been a period of robust economic growth and higher interest rates around the world.
"There is tentative evidence of this happening with AI; our estimates for the neutral rate have risen in recent years, and bond yields have increased over the past couple of months with market participants citing strong demand for capital as a key driver," she said.
"Firms want to invest to take advantage of the new technology and to expand their capacity to meet faster future growth.
"Given this is happening globally, they'll be competing for scarce savings, pushing up interest rates."
Hunter said there was limited evidence yet of an AI-led lift in productivity, and that this was might be due to businesses taking time to invest and reorganise their operations to take full benefit of the technology. But this could change.
"This experience mirrors that of previous general-purpose technologies. Their implementation typically led to what economists call a productivity J-curve," she said.
"One example is electricity. The largest productivity gains did not come simply from replacing steam engines with electric motors, but from reorganising production and redesigning factory processes to best suit this new source of energy."
An ongoing concern is that AI will wipe out occupations, forcing many people out of work.
Hunter said there was little evidence the technology had affected overall employment, but she said there were signs of lower hiring among younger workers in "highly AI-exposed occupations".
"In Australia, contacts in the RBA's liaison program indicate that AI has not yet impacted most firms' headcount and is not expected to over the next year," she said.
The impact of AI on the Australian economy has prompted the RBA to devote more of its resources on its economic ramifications. Yesterday, the bank released four separate pieces of new research into AI.
One research paper suggests 5.3 per cent of Australian households' financial wealth, estimated at almost $9 trillion, is invested in AI-related companies either directly or through superannuation. In late 2022, it was just 2 per cent.
Separate research shows the bank expects $115 billion to be invested in Australia in data centres by 2028, or about 2 per cent of GDP per year, not including supporting infrastructure such as energy sources for the data centres.
Data centre demand for energy has meant some renewable energy projects that may not have been financially viable are being built. But the RBA research said the strong growth for electricity by data centres "could place upward pressure on wholesale electricity prices for a time".
In last week's US midterm elections, 40 initiatives were on county and state ballots relating to data centres. All proposals to restrict data centres succeeded.
Hunter said the benefits of AI were unlikely to be distributed across the community evenly. Financial returns so far are flowing to a small number of businesses and their equity holders.
"Some workers may face a difficult period of adjustment as demand for particular roles or tasks decline, which will weigh on income and spending by some households," she said. "The strength of the consumption response will depend not only on the overall increase in income, but also on how broadly the gains are shared across the economy and the pathway for integrating the technology into our daily lives."
